1:
How many sons Ahab had, and in what sense they were his, is the first question. Gill allows that these might not all be immediate sons but some of them grandsons, as such are sometimes called in Scripture, and Henry writes "seventy sons (or grandsons)" with the same reserve. Ellicott takes the posterity in general to be meant: Ahab had been dead some fourteen years and had had two successors on the throne (2 Kings 3:1; 1 Kings 22:51), so that the name stands here for the house of Ahab — though many of the number may have been strictly his, since he no doubt had a considerable harem. Clarke argues from the same polygamy, setting the figure beside Rehoboam's thirty-eight sons, Abdon's forty, Tola's thirty and Gideon's seventy-one. Henry notices that seventy is Gideon's number (Judges 8:30) and draws the lesson that such a quiver full of arrows could not protect Ahab's house from divine vengeance — numerous families, if vicious, must not expect to be long prosperous.

To whom the letters went is a textual problem rather than a historical one. The received text says the rulers of Jezreel; Clarke replies that it certainly should be the rulers of Samaria, since the whole context shows that to them and to that city the letters were sent. Ellicott calls "Jezreel" an ancient error, noting that the Greek and Josephus read Samaria, that Thenius would restore "and sent from Jezreel to the princes of Samaria," and that Reuss reads Israel for Jezreel; his own preference is the Latin's "to the chief men of the city," with "and unto" restored before "the elders" on manuscript authority.

Who the guardians were explains why Jehu wrote to them at all. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as them who brought up Ahab — that is, his house — the word being the one used of a nursing father (Numbers 11:12; Isaiah 49:23), and reasons that nobles so entrusted would be answerable for their wards' good behaviour, Ahab perhaps dreading an education in the harem and disputes about the succession. Clarke takes the custom as established, the royal children of Israel and Judah being entrusted to the nobles, and supposes the prophet's word about kings as nursing fathers and queens as nursing mothers alludes to it. Henry adds a darker note: those still under tuition had tutors charged with an education agreeable to their birth, but it is to be feared they were brought up in the idolatries of their father's house.

That the letter is sarcasm nobody doubts. Clarke says no reader need be told these letters were all ironical, and spells out the real message — you have no means of defence, Israel is with me, and if you do not yield up yourselves and the city I will put you all to the sword. Ellicott hears a tone of mocking irony, pointing out that by carefully enumerating the nobles' resources Jehu as good as says his defiance is not the fruit of ignorance; and judges them as luxurious and cowardly then as in the days of Amos a few years later (Amos 6:3). Henry reads the challenge as upbraiding, not invitation: Jehu did not desire them to set up one of Ahab's sons but said in effect, do if you dare, and see what will come of it — those who have forsaken their religion having often, with it, lost both sense and courage. Keil and Delitzsch record only that the ruse had the desired result.

Two points of wording close the paragraph. On "a fenced city" Ellicott observes that every version but the Arabic has the plural, as Josephus does, where Clarke takes the whole description to refer to Samaria alone, in which the magazines and implements of war were kept.
4:
The fear is doubled in the Hebrew. Ellicott translates literally "And they feared mightily, mightily," the idiom of the flood narrative (Genesis 7:19), and notes that in what they say next the word kings is emphatic — rather "the two kings," the two they had just watched fall. Gill explains what they had seen: the purport of the letters, that should they attempt anything of the kind Jehu would come upon them with his forces, which intimidated them at once.

Their reasoning Henry puts into their own mouths. Two kings stood not before him but fell as sacrifices to his rage; how then shall we stand? So they sent him a surrender of themselves — we are thy servants, thy subjects, and will do all that thou shalt bid us, right or wrong, and will set up nobody in competition with thee. They saw it was to no purpose to contend with him, and therefore it was their interest to submit. Henry then turns the argument upward: with much more reason may we argue ourselves into subjection to the great God, before whose wrath many kings and great men have fallen for their wickedness; do we provoke the LORD to jealousy, are we stronger than he? We must either bend or break. Keil and Delitzsch report the same exchange flatly — the ruse had the desired result, and the messengers announced submission with no desire to appoint a king.

Who sent the answer is set out by office. Gill takes him that was over the house for the keeper of the king's palace in Samaria, with the custody, care and government of it; Wesley calls him the chief governor of the palace. Ellicott names him the prefect of the palace, or major-domo, observes that a similar official appears on the Egyptian monuments, and compares his position and influence with those of the great chamberlain of the Byzantine court. Him that was over the city Ellicott makes the prefect or governor, the man called the prince of the city earlier in the history (1 Kings 22:26), and he identifies these two as the "rulers" to whom the letters were addressed; Wesley allows either the chief magistrate or the military governor.

Clarke reads the submission as complete and already culpable: thus all the constituted authorities agreed to submit, making no conditions, and so stood pledged to commit the horrid murders which this most execrable man afterwards commanded.
6:
Clarke takes one word of the second letter as settling a question raised by the first: "come to me to Jezreel" shows that the letters were not written to Jezreel but from Jezreel to Samaria. Ellicott measures that journey at more than twenty miles, and reads the deadline as urgency — time was all-important to Jehu, who wanted the people of Jezreel convinced as soon as possible that no royal prince was left to claim the crown and that the nobles of Samaria had joined his cause. Gill says only that he wrote again having gained his point by the former letter.

The order itself Ellicott will not soften: Jehu knew his men, and the cool cynicism of his savage command is worthy of a Sulla or a Marius. Of the obedience Henry asks the questions the narrative does not — could they betray such a trust, could they be cruel to their master's sons? So low did they stoop in their adoration of the rising sun that they did it, and Gill notes they did not in the least hesitate but complied immediately. Learn from it, Henry says, not to trust in a friend nor put confidence in a guide not governed by conscience, for one can scarcely expect that he who has been false to his God should ever be faithful to his prince. Then he observes God's righteousness in their unrighteousness: these same men had been wickedly obsequious to Jezebel's order for the murder of Naboth (1 Kings 21:11), and she, it is likely, gloried in the power she had over them — so let none aim at arbitrary power, lest they be found rolling a stone which some time or other will return upon them. Princes who make their people slaves take the readiest way to make them rebels.

The verdicts on the deed divide sharply. Clarke's is a single exclamation: what cold-blooded wretches were the whole of these people. Wesley divides the guilt — Jehu justly required this, because the sovereign Lord of all men's lives had commanded it, but the Samaritans wickedly obeyed, without any knowledge of or regard to God's command. Ellicott finds the historian's own judgement in his diction: the verb is better rendered butchered or slaughtered, and the way he writes that they took the king's sons and butchered seventy persons shows he did not sympathise with Jehu's deeds of blood, his interest centring rather on the fulfilment of Elijah's predictions by Jehu's wickedness.

The clause naming the victims is unsettled in the manuscripts. Ellicott renders it literally as the heads of the men of the sons of your master, and lists what the witnesses do with it: some manuscripts, the Syriac, Arabic and Latin, and the copies Origen mentions, omit "men"; Thenius keeps the word, taking it to mark that only male descendants were to die; the Alexandrian Greek omits "sons"; four Hebrew manuscripts read "house" instead. The Authorised Version, he allows, is a permissible interpretation. Some witnesses also give "a second letter" for "the second time," and the Greek has "bring them" for "come," which he calls a natural conjecture. As for the number, he doubts it should be pressed — seventy is a favourite round number.

The closing clause is a parenthesis. Ellicott defends the Authorised Version's rendering of it and rejects the alternative the Masoretic punctuation might allow, the particle in question being very doubtfully used that way; the sentence is in any case only a parenthetic reminder of what the chapter's opening had already said. Keil and Delitzsch pass straight on to the baskets, which they have the nobles fill willingly; Ellicott notes that the word for them means a pot elsewhere (1 Samuel 2:14) and that the Greek translators rendered it one way in the Psalms and here by a word for pointed baskets.
8:
The heads arrive at night. Clarke infers the hour from the order that followed, and reads the order as calculated: Jehu had them left at the gate, a place of public resort, so that all the people might see them, be struck with terror, and conclude that resistance to such authority and power would be vain. Ellicott renders the opening literally as "and the messenger came in," notes that Josephus has Jehu at a banquet when he came, and makes something of the word for heaps — it occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament, its verb means to heap up (Exodus 8:10), and in the Talmud the noun means a congregation, much as we say colloquially a heap of persons. Where the heaps stood he leaves open: the gate is the place of public business, where every citizen would see them (1 Kings 22:10), but perhaps the palace gate rather than the city gate is meant. Henry calls it the proper place of judgment. Parallels, Ellicott adds, are not wanting — in the history of modern Persia, and in the comparatively recent custom in our own country of fixing the heads of traitors on London Bridge.

"Ye be righteous" is the hinge of Jehu's speech, and three senses are offered for it. Ellicott's own is that the people are guiltless in respect of these deaths and therefore have nothing to dread; Thenius takes it as "ye are just, and therefore will judge justly"; others read it as a question, "are ye righteous?", on the view that Jehu wished to make the people guilty of the massacre of the princes while owning only his own murder of the king. Clarke hears another irony, intended partly to excuse himself and partly to involve them in the odium of the massacre, while justifying the conduct of both by showing that all was done according to the commandment of the LORD. Henry takes the words at face value as an acquittal — there Jehu acquitted the people before God and the world — and sees him acquitting himself comparatively by the same stroke: I slew but one, they have slain all these; I did it by conspiracy and with design, they have done this merely in compliance. It is common, Henry remarks, for those who have done something base to attempt the mitigation of their own reproach by drawing others in to do something worse.

The question that follows is self-exculpation. Ellicott would render the verb smote rather than slew, has the pronoun emphatic — I on my part — and takes Jehu to be professing astonishment: he hints that since the LORD had foretold the destruction of Ahab's house, the LORD must have brought it to pass, and therefore nobody is to blame. Of his posture Ellicott reports Reuss's reading, that he took his place as judge in the palace gateway after the royal custom and gave audience to the people, who would naturally have crowded to the gates in consternation at the two ghastly pyramids before the palace.
10:
What Jehu asks them to know Gill makes a lesson in providence: all this, and what else should follow of the same kind, was brought about by the providence of God according to divine predictions, as just punishment on Ahab's family for their sins — so that neither Jehu nor others were to be blamed, being only instruments the LORD made use of. Ellicott glosses the falling to the earth as the falling of a dead thing, man, bird or beast (Matthew 10:29), insists no part of Elijah's prediction shall fail of accomplishment, and would render the last clause "and Jehovah, He hath done it." Henry resolves the whole into the righteous judgment of God, with a caution: God is not the author of any man's sin, but even by what men do from bad principles he serves his own purposes and glorifies his own name, being righteous in the very thing wherein men are unrighteous — as when the Assyrian is made the rod of his anger and the instrument of his justice, and yet meaneth not so, neither does his heart think so (Isaiah 10:7).

The massacre then widens, and Keil and Delitzsch note the effect of the speech: the people looked quietly on. Henry lists the victims — not only those descended from Ahab but all in any relation to him, the officers of his household, the ministers of state and those in command under him, his kinsfolk and acquaintance who had been partners in his wickedness, and his priests or domestic chaplains, who strengthened his hand that he should not turn from his evil way. Ellicott would read "and" for "so," renders kinsfolk as his friends, literally his known ones, and glosses the great men as high officials who owed their exaltation to Ahab. On the priests Keil and Delitzsch take court priests to be meant, of the kind the heathen kings had, and refuse Thenius's secular counsellors or nearest servants — a sense, they say, the Hebrew word never has. Clarke draws a further inference, that the great men who had so obsequiously taken off the heads of Ahab's seventy sons fell a sacrifice in their turn to the ambition of this incomparably bad man. Henry closes with a warning against the precedent: this was bloody work, and is not in any case to be drawn into one — let the guilty suffer, but not the guiltless for their sakes.
12:
Even the verse's first three verbs are disputed. The common Hebrew text has Jehu arise, come, and depart, which Keil and Delitzsch admit looks pleonastic; Ellicott judges the Syriac right in reading simply that he arose and came. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the transposition Böttcher and Thenius propose after that same Syriac, and for a reason of substance rather than style: moving the words would transfer the slaying of Ahaziah's relations to Samaria, which the next paragraph of the chapter contradicts. Their own account keeps the sequence loose — Jehu did not go straight to Samaria, but did what follows on the way. Gill supplies the errand he was on: to make a clear riddance there of all that belonged to Ahab, as at Jezreel, and to abolish idolatry.

The meeting-place has a name nobody can quite fix. Clarke takes it for the place where the shepherds met for the annual sheep shearing, and Keil and Delitzsch call it the binding-house of the shepherds. Ellicott keeps the Hebrew, Beth-eqed-haroim, and reports the Targum's "shepherds' meeting-house," most likely a solitary building serving as a rendezvous for the shepherds of the neighbourhood. The root, he explains, means to bind or knot together, whence the usual rendering "binding house," where they bound their sheep for shearing — though the idea of binding passes easily into that of gathering, as our own words band and knot do. The Greek has Baithakad of the shepherds, and Eusebius names a Beithakad fifteen Roman miles from Legio, which Ellicott identifies with the modern Beitkad six miles east of Jenin in the plain of Esdraelon; but that, he objects, seems too far off the road from Jezreel to Samaria, which passes Jenin.

Whose brethren these were is settled the same way by everyone. Gill makes them the sons of Ahaziah's brethren, called his brethren as Lot was called Abraham's brother, since his own brothers had been slain by the Arabians before he came to the throne. Clarke says the term among the Jews covered the relatives of one family, especially brothers' and sisters' children, and points to the parallel account for proof. Ellicott agrees that Ahaziah's kinsmen are meant, his brothers in the strict sense having fallen to a troop of Arabs in his father Jehoram's lifetime (2 Chronicles 21:17; 2 Chronicles 22:8). Henry adds three grounds on which they came within Jehu's commission: they were branches of Ahab's house, being descended from Athaliah; they were tainted with that house's wickedness; and they were at that moment on their way to pay court to it.

Their errand Ellicott reconstructs closely. "We go down" is rather we have come down, and to salute is to inquire after their health; the children of the king are Joram's sons, and the children of the queen are literally the sons of the mistress — that is, of the queen-mother Jezebel, and so Joram's brothers — both sets being among the sons of Ahab whom Jehu had already destroyed. News of the taking of Ramoth and of Joram's recovery may have reached Jerusalem and drawn these princes on a visit of pleasure to the court at Jezreel, not suspecting what had happened meanwhile with the headlong rapidity characteristic of Jehu. Clarke makes the same point as a verdict on Jehu's speed: so promptly had he executed all his measures that the nearest relatives of the murdered kings had not even heard of their death, and so had no time to escape — they were all taken as in a net.
14: "Take them alive" Gill reads as an order to the guards to seize them and make them captives; Ellicott wonders whether they made some show of resistance. Why they died at all he puts down to their connection with the doomed house, while reporting that Keil rather supposes Jehu dreaded their conspiring with the partisans of the fallen dynasty in Samaria. The execution Ellicott renders literally as slaughtered them into the cistern of Betheked, and allows two pictures of it: either they cut their throats over the cistern or threw the corpses in. Clarke guesses the pit was where the sheep were washed before shearing, or the fleeces after. Henry has the forty-two appointed as sheep for the sacrifice and slain with solemnity, and Ellicott notes the number is curiously parallel to another in this book, and may be a definite standing for an indefinite one (2 Kings 2:24).
15:
Jehonadab is introduced by his clan. Ellicott explains that "the son of Rechab" means the Rechabite (1 Chronicles 2:55), and relays Ewald's view that the Rechabites were one of the new societies formed after Elijah's departure for the active support of the true religion — their founder in that sense being Jonadab, who, despairing of practising the legitimate worship within the community, retired into the desert with his followers and, like Israel of old, preferred the rough life of tents to all the allurements of city life. Only unusual circumstances, he adds, could draw them back into the circle of common life. Wesley calls him a Kenite and a man of singular prudence and piety, come to congratulate Jehu on the destruction of that wicked family and to encourage him to go on fulfilling the will of God. Henry makes the same point from the charge Jehonadab laid on his posterity, which they religiously observed three hundred years after, not to drink wine nor dwell in cities (Jeremiah 35:6): a man mortified to the world and meddling little with its business, no prophet, priest or Levite, no prince or ruler, but eminent for prudence and piety and generally respected — and Jehu, though a soldier, knew him and honoured him. The countenance of good men, Henry remarks, is a thing great men will value if they are wise (Psalms 119:79).

The question Jehu puts is textually awkward. Ellicott reports the Hebrew as "Is there with thy heart right?", which does not agree with the rest of the sentence; some manuscripts drop the offending particle, and he thinks the original reading is probably preserved in the Vatican Greek, "Is thy heart right with my heart, as my heart with thy heart?", which secures a parallelism the Syriac also keeps. Clarke renders the sense freely — art thou with me in the prosecution of a reform in Israel, as my heart is with thine in the true religion of Jehovah and the destruction of Baal? — and Wesley shortens it further: dost thou heartily approve of me and my present proceedings? Henry turns it on the reader: Is thy heart right? is a question we should often put to ourselves, for a man may make a fair profession and gain a reputation among men and still not be inward with God.

What the giving of the hand amounted to is disputed. Ellicott takes it as a pledge of good faith and a token of amity, striking hands being the way a compact was sealed (Isaiah 2:6). Henry agrees and goes further: Jehonadab gave his word and gave his hand as a pledge of his heart, yielding to Jehu in the sense the phrase bears elsewhere (2 Chronicles 30:8), and so concurred and covenanted with him, owning him in the work both of revenge and of reformation. Clarke will not have it: this has generally been taken for exacting a promise, but does it mean any more than taking him by the hand to help him step into the chariot in which Jehu was sitting?
16:
The ride itself Henry reads as an exchange of credit. Ellicott notes a variant in the clause, the Syriac, Greek and Arabic reading that he made him ride where the Hebrew and Targum have they made him ride — which may mean that Jehu’s followers helped Jehonadab, probably an aged sheikh, to mount. Jehu put some honour on Jehonadab by taking him into the chariot, which he was not accustomed to; but he received more honour than he gave, since all sober people would think the better of Jehu for seeing Jehonadab beside him. This was not the only time, Henry adds, that the piety of some has been made to serve the policy of others, designing men strengthening themselves by drawing good men into their interests. Ellicott says the same without the censure: it was important to Jehu to be seen acting in concert with a man revered for sanctity and powerful as a leader of the orthodox party, and he addresses him as a notoriously staunch adherent of the old faith.

The invitation to look on at his zeal is where the voices turn hostile. Ellicott would render it "look on at" rather than "see." Gill says it savours very much of vainglory, hypocrisy and a pharisaical spirit. Clarke breaks off into apostrophe — thou ostentatious and murderous hypocrite, thou hast zeal for Jehovah and his pure religion? witness thy calves at Dan and Bethel, and the general profligacy of thy conduct — and lays down a maxim: he who can call another to witness his zeal for religion, or his works of charity, has as much of both as serves his own turn. Henry brings two charges, that Jehu boasted of his zeal and that he wanted it seen and taken notice of, like the Pharisees who did all to be seen of men, since an upright heart approves itself to God and covets no more than his acceptance; but Henry stops short of a verdict — whether Jehu looked any further we cannot judge. Keil and Delitzsch keep the question of motive apart from the question of law: considered objectively, the slaying of the worshippers of Baal was in accordance with the law and, on the theocratic principle, perfectly right.
17:
Samaria falls in a single clause, which Ellicott renders literally as "and he entered Samaria, and smote." Here again, he notes, the name Ahab stands for the house or family so called, as some manuscripts and the Syriac make explicit by reading "the house of Ahab" (1 Kings 15:29). Gill fills in who was meant: all who were in any connection with Ahab, whether as relations of his family or as ministers of his in civil or religious things. Henry supposes Jehonadab went along and, likely enough, animated and assisted Jehu in this further execution of his commission — and he defends the possibility of such a man doing so, since one may hate cruelty and yet love justice, and be far from thirsting after blood and yet wash his feet in the blood of the wicked (Psalms 58:10).

"Ahab served Baal a little; but Jehu shall serve him much" is the chapter's hardest saying, and the readings of it diverge. Clarke supplies a motive: Jehu had determined that no worship should remain in Israel but that of the golden calves at Dan and Bethel, so to destroy the worshippers of Baal without suspicion he proclaimed a great sacrifice, and to destroy them the more easily he gathered them all into one place. Ellicott hears not a falsehood but a double meaning — Ahab had, as the people well knew, served Baal more than a little, yet the antithesis was not too strong for Jehu's hidden sense, since he was thinking of the holocaust of human victims he intended. Henry weighs three possibilities: that Jehu spoke ironically, or to try whether the body of the people would oppose such a resolution, or — as he thinks more likely — purposely to deceive the worshippers of Baal, in which case it cannot be justified, for the truth of God needs not any man's lie. Wesley allows no latitude at all: the words being manifestly false and spoken with a design to deceive cannot be excused, on the immovable principle that we must not do the least evil that the greatest good may come. Keil and Delitzsch simply call it a pretence of wishing to serve Baal even more than Ahab had done.

The summons that follows is comprehensive by design. Ellicott sets it beside Elijah's convocation of the prophets of Baal and of the Asherah (1 Kings 18:19), and observes that the word rendered "his servants" is the same one rendered "worshippers" further down. Gill distributes the three classes: the prophets were employed in invocation of Baal and in singing praises to him, the priests in offering sacrifice, and the servants or ministers in assisting them. The threat attached to absence Clarke reads as a trap baited with piety — whoever stayed away would thereby show himself without zeal for the service of his god, and so would justly forfeit his life.

The historian's own word for the manoeuvre is the one Ellicott lingers over. It means in guile, or treacherously, and it occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament; it is connected with the proper name Jacob (Genesis 25:26; Hosea 12:4), and the Greek translators rendered it literally as "in heeling" — that is, striking with the heel, tripping up. Clarke's verdict on the whole proceeding is of a piece with it: all this was done in the very spirit of deceit. Keil and Delitzsch state the end it served without comment on the means — the festival was appointed so that the worshippers of Baal might be destroyed.
20:
The proclamation is couched in the language of true religion. Ellicott would render it "sanctify a solemn meeting" (Isaiah 1:13), and points out what that laid on the invited: everyone who wished to attend would have to sanctify, or purify, himself in due form. Gill explains the institution behind it — among the Jews a holy convocation was a day on which they were restrained from doing any work — and supposes Jehu meant exactly such a day for Baal, so that the people might be at leisure to attend. Notice went out by criers through all Israel, Ellicott adds, and Gill has Jehu send men for the purpose.

Henry describes the mood of those who answered. The bigoted and besotted Baalites began to think themselves very happy, and that now they should see golden days again; Joram had put away the image of Baal (2 Kings 3:2), and if Jehu would restore it they had what they wanted, so they came up to Samaria with joy from all parts to celebrate the solemnity, pleased to see the house of Baal crowded and his priests in their vestments. Ellicott pauses over a textual curiosity: the Vatican Greek adds a sentence repeating the summons and its death penalty, which he takes for a marginal note belonging elsewhere that found its way into the text — preserving, on Thenius's account, the earlier verse's reading from another manuscript.

How full the house was is a question of metaphor. Keil and Delitzsch derive the Hebrew word not from the noun for a corner, as Gesenius did, but from the word for a mouth, meaning the upper rim of a vessel, and give the figure as one taken from vessels filled with liquid. Ellicott arrives at the same picture — the rim of the contents reached the rim of the vessel, as if we were to say the house was brimful — while recording that Schulz explained it "head to head," Gesenius "from corner to corner," and the Greek translated it literally "mouth to mouth." The Authorised Version, he judges, has the sense right.

The officer of the wardrobe is named by a word nobody can place. Ellicott observes that it occurs here only: the Targum takes it for chests or caskets, the Greek leaves it untranslated, the Syriac makes the man a treasurer, the Latin has those who were over the vestments, and Thenius thinks it means no more than a cell or storechamber. An Ethiopic word for a linen robe is said to be connected with it, which would make "vestry" literally right — and Clarke traces the English word back through vestiarium to the verb for clothing, so that it properly names the place where sacerdotal robes and ornaments are kept. Gill simply calls the man the keeper of the garments in which the priests of Baal ministered.

Whose garments they were is the live question. Keil and Delitzsch rule out the king's palace, from which Thenius would have Jehu supply every participant with a festal dress, and argue for the wardrobe of the temple of Baal, since the priests of Baal had their own sacred dresses as the priests of almost all religions did — Silius says as much of the priests of the Gadetanic Hercules. Ellicott thinks it more natural still that Jehu was simply directing all the priests and prophets to be careful to wear their distinctive dress at a festival meant to be a specially great one, the phrase being literally "the vestments," those customary on such occasions. Clarke notes that the priests of Baal had their robes as the priests of the LORD had theirs, but that the two were easily distinguished; and Henry supposes the worshippers too had some badge to notify their relation to Baal, since there were vestments for all of them.
23:
Where Jehu and Jehonadab went Ellicott locates precisely: into the outer court before the temple, where all the worshippers were waiting. Gill draws the inference the narrative invites about the companion — Jehonadab was no doubt let into the secret and knew the design, or he would never have entered such an idolatrous place — and Henry has him own Jehu in the work of reformation as well as of revenge.

The order to search out the worshippers of the LORD is the trap's finest piece of work, and each voice says why. Ellicott puts the matter in terms of how it looked: the precaution suggests suspicion to a modern reader, but to the Baal-worshippers it would have suggested the very contrary — an extraordinary reverence for Baal, and a dread lest a profane person should be present in his sanctuary. Clarke reads Jehu's own position oddly but consistently: he was not attached to the service of the LORD, yet he would tolerate it, and since he supposed himself to be fulfilling the will of Jehovah he would treat that worship and its worshippers with the more respect. The pretext, Clarke adds, fitted heathen custom, which excluded the profane whenever an extraordinary manifestation of a god was expected — as Callimachus, imagining the temple and its precinct shaken by the approach of Apollo, breaks off into a cry against the profane. Without such a plea, alarm must have been excited and some would have escaped. Henry agrees that the Baalites took it for a provision to keep their worship from being profaned by strangers, and marvels that they did not see themselves brought into a snare by it: no wonder that those who suffer themselves to be deceived by Baal, as all idolaters were by their idols, should be deceived by Jehu to their destruction.

The sacrifice proper is staged in an inner space. Ellicott has the priests and prophets go into the inner court of the temple, which probably resembled in general construction the house of the LORD at Jerusalem, and notes that peace offerings and burnt offerings could only be offered in an open court. Of the guard he would correct the tense — rather, now Jehu had set fourscore men on the outside of the building. Henry pictures the same arrangement as a sealing of the exits: a strict search within, lest any servant of God should have got among them for company or curiosity and any wheat be mixed with those tares, and eighty men posted at all the avenues to Baal's temple that none might escape.

The injunction laid on those eighty is rough in the Hebrew. Ellicott renders it literally — the man that escapeth of the men whom I am bringing into your hands, his life for his life — and allows it to be a little incoherent, as is natural in energetic speech, though the sense is clear. Thenius would repoint the verb as a transitive, giving "the man that letteth escape any of the men," which Ellicott calls an improvement that may be right, while observing that the old versions agree with the present Hebrew pointing. Keil and Delitzsch adopt that very correction without hesitation, reading the transitive form and construing the threat as life for life in the sense the phrase bears elsewhere in the book of Kings (1 Kings 20:39): whoever lets one of the men escape whom Jehu puts into their hands shall answer for him with his own life.
25:
Who made an end of offering the burnt offering is not agreed. Gill takes it for the chief of the priests of Baal, whose office that service was; Keil and Delitzsch read the pronoun the same way — the sacrificing priest, not Jehu — while allowing that the singular may be indefinite, as if it said when one had finished. Ellicott thinks the Syriac right in putting it in the plural, when they, the Baal priests, had made an end, and refuses Ewald's supposition that Jehu personally offered sacrifice in the character of an ardent Baal-worshipper; what Jehu chose was the moment, when the whole assembly was absorbed in worship. Clarke alone writes as though Jehu did offer it, and makes the point a moral one: had he been a man of any conscientious principle in religion he would have finished the tragedy before offering, but to a man of no religion the worship of Jehovah and of Baal are alike, and if he prefers either it is merely as a statesman, for political purposes.

The men he called in are named by their ranks. Ellicott renders them literally the runners, or couriers, and the adjutants, or squires — the royal guardsmen and their officers. Clarke keeps the Hebrew of the second term, explaining it as the men of the third rank, officers next below the nobles, with only the king and the nobles above them; the runners he guesses to have been a sort of light infantry.

The order itself Keil and Delitzsch give flatly: come and smite them, without one coming out — whereupon the guardsmen smote them with the edge of the sword and slew them unsparingly. Henry adds the grim symmetry he sees in it: their blood was mingled with their sacrifices by way of just revenge, as they themselves had sometimes done when, in their blind devotion, they cut themselves with knives and lancets till the blood gushed out (1 Kings 18:28). The doing of it, he judges, though seemingly barbarous, was, considering the nature of their crime, really righteous — for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.

What happened next turns on two words. "Cast them out" the Targum and the other versions take for throwing the dead bodies out of the temple, and Ellicott with them; Thenius asks why that should be specially mentioned and would read the verb intransitively, "rushed out," which Ellicott admits suits very well with what follows. The place they went to is called the city of the house of Baal, and here the readings part company. Ellicott gives the word its original sense of citadel or stronghold, properly a place surrounded by a ring-fence or rampart, and has the guards rush up the steps into the sanctuary itself, which like Solomon's temple resembled a fortress — a reading he supports from Sebastian Schmidt and traces, for the word's obscure Hebrew origin, to the cuneiform. Gesenius made it the sacred enclosure of the temple, which Ellicott says does not suit the context. Clarke asks instead whether it does not mean a sort of holy of holies where the most sacred images of Baal were kept, separated from the temple as the holy of holies was from the holy place. Wesley takes it for the buildings belonging to the house of Baal, numerous and capacious enough to be called a city, in some of which the priests of Baal or of the groves may have dwelt (1 Kings 18:19).
26:
What was brought out and burned is described in the plural. Gill calls them lesser images, those of other deities or decorations of the temple. Keil and Delitzsch identify them as wooden columns, attendant or altar-companion figures of Baal rather than the god himself. Ellicott would render the word pillars throughout, wooden and of sacred significance (Hosea 3:4), and quotes Cheyne: in primitive times a pillar was the distinguishing mark of a holy place, and though idolatrous pillars were commanded to be destroyed (Exodus 23:24), pillars to Jehovah are reckoned to have been allowable much later, the prophet even sanctioning one in Egypt (Isaiah 19:19). The Greek has the singular here and the plural next, Ellicott notes; the Syriac keeps the singular in both.

The one broken rather than burned is distinguished from the rest. Ellicott takes it for the conical pillar of stone representing the Baal himself, the wooden pillars of the previous verse symbolising companion deities; Keil and Delitzsch say the same, citing Movers — the column of Baal was the real image, probably a conical stone dedicated to him, while those burned were his wooden attendants. Who the god was Gill leaves open: some take him for Belus, others Saturn, others the sun, which he thinks most probable. Henry runs the whole demolition together — the buildings about the house of Baal, where his priests and their families lived, so many and so stately that the text calls them a city; all the little images, statues, pictures and shrines that beautified it; and with them the great image of Baal himself.

What the temple became is put so bluntly that the Hebrew was softened. Keil and Delitzsch report that the Masoretes substituted a euphemism for the original word, which means privies — the thing itself a mark of the greatest insult, of which many examples are met with among Oriental peoples (Ezra 6:11; Daniel 2:5). Clarke will not soften it: a place for human excrement, as all the versions understand it, and nothing more degrading — he made it a public necessary. Ellicott calls it utter desecration (Ezekiel 6:11), and notes that the phrase "unto this day" raises a question of its own about the book’s date. Henry reads the purpose in it: made a dunghill, the common sink or sewer of the city, that the remembrance of it might be blotted out or made infamous.

The summary verse draws the sharpest division of judgement. Gill measures the extent — Baal’s images and temples were served thus in all places throughout Israel where there were any. Henry measures it against what had been: the worship had once prevailed so far that there were but seven thousand of all the thousands of Israel who had not bowed the knee to Baal, and those concealed; so, he says, will God destroy all the gods of the heathen and sooner or later triumph over them. Keil and Delitzsch set the achievement beside what Jehu left standing: he exterminated the worship of Baal, but the sins of Jeroboam, the golden calves at Bethel and Dan — that is, the idolatrous worship of Jehovah — he allowed to remain, and with this remark the history of his reign opens the last epoch of the ten tribes. Ellicott separates the act from the motive: objectively the slaughter of the servants of Baal was in perfect harmony with the Law, but subjectively the motive was thoroughly selfish, since the priests and prophets of Baal, depending entirely on the dynasty of the king who had introduced their worship, might prove dangerous to him; by exterminating them he might hope to secure the allegiance of the party that stood by the legitimate worship. His keeping up the worship Jeroboam established proves, Ellicott concludes, that he acted from policy rather than religious zeal.
29:
The qualifying word opening the verse carries weight. Ellicott renders it simply "only," the term the compiler uses constantly to qualify his estimate of a king's conduct (2 Kings 12:3; 2 Kings 14:4), so that the verse is a parenthetic qualification of the approval just implied. Gill takes the description of Jeroboam for that king's standing character, a blot never to be wiped off. Henry sets the two idolatries side by side: the worship of Baal was the greater evil and more heinous in God's sight, yet it weakened Israel and made them beholden to the Sidonians, so Jehu could easily part with it; the worship of the calves was a politic idolatry, begun and kept up for reasons of state, to prevent the return of the ten tribes to the house of David, and so he clave to it. True conversion, Henry draws out, is not only from wasteful sins but from gainful ones — not only from those destructive to the secular interest but from those that support and befriend it, in forsaking which is the great trial whether we can deny ourselves and trust God. Ellicott says the same without the moral: Jehu maintained the worship at Bethel and Dan on the same grounds of state policy as the kings before him. Wesley puts it shortest: his religion was plainly superficial, or it would not have given way to his policy.

The commendation that follows is harder to place, and every voice qualifies it somewhere. Henry begins with the censures Jehu must have drawn: many, it is probable, called him a rebel, a usurper and a murderer, and prognosticated ill of a family so raised; but God said, Well done, and it signified little who said otherwise. He grants that it is justly questionable whether Jehu acted from a good principle, or took some false steps in the doing of it; yet the extirpating of idolaters and idolatry was right in God's eyes, and Jehu went through with his work. Keil and Delitzsch make the distinction exactly: the divine sentence refers to the deed as such and not to the subjective motives by which Jehu was actuated, since it is obvious from the limitation added in the next verse that the deed had not sprung from pure zeal for the honour of the LORD. Wesley compresses the whole qualification into four words — done well in part, and so far as is here expressed.

Who carried the message is not stated, and two guesses are offered. Gill reasons that it came by a prophet, Jehu not being one, and reports that the Jews generally suppose this to have been Jonah the son of Amittai; Ellicott suggests Elisha instead. Ellicott notes that the Syriac and Arabic supply a conjunction the Hebrew lacks before "hast done," and sets the promise beside the commandment’s visiting of the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation (Exodus 20:5) — the same reckoning turned into a blessing.

The four generations are counted out. Clarke names them — Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam the second, and Zechariah — and adds a bleak gloss: this was all the compensation Jehu had in either world for his zeal. Henry measures the promise against the dynasty Jehu had destroyed: of the house of Ahab there were indeed four kings, Omri, Ahab, Ahaziah and Joram, but the last two were brothers, so that it reached only to the third generation, and the whole family lasted about forty-five years, whereas Jehu's continued in four besides himself, about a hundred and twenty years in all. No services done for God, he concludes, shall go unrewarded. Keil and Delitzsch tie the promise to the deed that earned it, the extermination of the godless royal house, and both they and Ellicott note where its fulfilment is recorded (2 Kings 15:12).
31:
Ellicott would begin a new paragraph here rather than at the next verse, rendering the opening "now Jehu had not been careful." The law meant is the Mosaic law, which forbids the use of images such as the calves, and "with all his heart" he takes to be explained by the clause that follows: Jehu had honoured Jehovah by extirpating the foreign Baal-worship, but supported the irregular worship of Jehovah that Jeroboam had established as the state religion of the north. The connecting "for," he notes, is not in the Hebrew.

What the negligence amounted to the others spell out. Gill applies it to his moral conversation: he was not careful that it should be according to the law of God, and what he did do agreeably to it was not done sincerely or from the right principle. Clarke is blunter — he never made it his study, indeed never intended to walk in this way, since it suited neither his disposition nor his politics. Henry divides the charge in two. Jehu showed no care: he lived at large, was not solicitous to please God or do his duty, took no heed to the scriptures, the prophets or his own conscience, but walked at all adventures — and the heedless, Henry fears, are graceless, since a good principle in the heart makes men circumspect. And he showed no zeal: what he did in religion he did not do with his heart, but as if he did it not, without any liveliness or concern. It seems, Henry concludes, he had little religion himself, and yet God made use of him as an instrument of reformation in Israel — a pity that those who do good to others should not always be good themselves.

The cutting short of Israel is worth pressing, and the versions pull two ways. Ellicott renders it literally as cutting off in Israel, that is, cutting off part after part of Israelite territory, the verb meaning properly to cut off the extremities (Proverbs 26:6), and Keil and Delitzsch read it as rending away certain portions from the kingdom. Clarke prefers the margin's "the Lord cut off the ends," which he says God did by permitting Hazael to seize the coasts and occupy the frontier towns. The Targum takes another line — the wrath of the LORD began to be strong against Israel — and the Latin agrees; Thenius would conjecture a Hebrew reading to match, which Ellicott rejects because the construction would then be unusual. "In all the coasts" he would render on the whole border, the border conterminous with Syria.

Why Hazael was the instrument is answered politically and theologically at once. Ellicott explains that Jehu, as a vassal and ally of Assyria, drew upon himself the active hostility of Hazael, and quotes Schröder: it was quite natural for the Israelite sovereign to throw himself into the arms of distant Assyria in order to get protection against his immediate neighbour Syria, Israel's hereditary foe — much as Ahaz would do later (2 Kings 16:7). But from the sacred writer's point of view, he adds, the verse states the consequence of Jehu's neglect, the LORD beginning the work through Hazael and the Syrians (Isaiah 10:5). Keil and Delitzsch supply the link the text leaves unstated: Hazael had now to inflict chastisement upon faithless Israel. Clarke identifies the ravages as the commencement of what Elisha had foretold (2 Kings 8:12). Gill notices the timing — the shrinking began under so active and courageous a king, so that the hand of God was the more seen in it — and Henry extends the blame beyond Jehu: when the king took no heed to God's law the people were as careless as he, so that they were short in their duty to God and God cut them short in extent, wealth and power.
33:
This verse maps what Hazael took. Ellicott says it defines the border land he ravaged and in fact occupied — the land east of the Jordan, all Gilead, the territory of Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh. Aroer on the Arnon, now Ara'ir, was Gilead's southern limit, the region reaching north to Mount Hermon and taking in Bashan; Keil and Delitzsch identify it as a ruin on the northern edge of the Arnon valley (Numbers 32:34). The closing words, "even Gilead and Bashan," Ellicott takes as added lest only Gilead in the narrower sense be supposed: the whole land east of the Jordan was conquered.

What the conquest was like, and when, is handled separately. Ellicott calls Hazael's conquests ones of great barbarity, pointing to the prophet's charge against Damascus (Amos 1:3) and Elisha's prediction (2 Kings 8:12); and he disputes Ewald's dating, which has Hazael take advantage of the internal troubles at the outset of the reign, since a man of Jehu's energy must soon have established domestic tranquillity. Henry makes Hazael above any other vexatious to Israel, making continual inroads on the countries beyond Jordan, which lay nearest him and most exposed — so that the Reubenites and Gadites now smarted for the choice their ancestors made of an inheritance on that side of the river, for which Moses had reproved them (Numbers 32:1). Hazael did what Elisha foretold he would do, Henry adds, and yet for doing it God had a quarrel with him and his kingdom.

The closing formula sends the reader elsewhere. Gill points to the book of chronicles in which the acts of the kings from Jeroboam onward were recorded, and Jehu's with them. Ellicott notes that some manuscripts with the Targum and the Latin omit the "all" before "his might," while the Greek adds a clause about his conspiracies. Henry finds a judgement in the formula: notice is taken in general of Jehu's might, but because he took no heed to serve God the memorials of his mighty enterprises are justly buried in oblivion.

Clarke turns that silence into an indictment, then a question. We have no chronicles in which anything further is spoken of this bad man: his reign was long, twenty-eight years, and yet we know nothing of it but the commencement — and for barbarity and hypocrisy Jehu has few parallels, as the baseness of the nobles of Samaria has seldom been equalled. Ahab's bloody house must be cut off, Clarke grants; but did God ever design that it should be done by these means? The men were no doubt wicked, and God permitted their iniquity to manifest itself in this way, so that his purpose that Ahab's house should no more reign was accomplished (1 Kings 21:19; 1 Kings 21:29). The cutting off of the family was decreed by divine justice; the means, or at least the manner of the doing, were not entirely of God's appointing — though the commission the young prophet gave Jehu was very extensive (2 Kings 9:7). Many things, Clarke concludes, seem attributed to God as the agent which he does not execute but only permits.

The reign's length comes last, and two reasons are given for it. Keil and Delitzsch find the order contrary to the usual custom of these books and account for it by the narrative's shape: Jehu's accession is nowhere expressly mentioned, the character of his reign having been given along with his anointing and the extermination of Ahab's dynasty. Ellicott reads the Hebrew's placing of "in Samaria" last as emphasis, marking that Jehu made Samaria, not Jezreel, the seat of his court. Gill notes what the figure amounts to — twenty-eight years, longer than any king of Israel had reigned — and of the burial says only that he died as his fathers did.
